children: MEXICO CITY--The Bank of Mexico lowered its benchmark interest rate in a split decision, saying it was a "one-time adjustment" and it expects to hold the rate steady for a prolonged period.

The five-member board of governors voted 3-2 to reduce the overnight interest-rate target by a quarter of a percentage point, to 6.25%, following three consecutive meetings on hold. Deputy governors Galia Borja and Jonathan Heath voted to leave the rate at 6.5%.
The central bank had been widely expected to leave the rate unchanged. Of 36 respondents in a survey by Citi Research this week, six predicted a rate cut.

"I think this came as a surprise to many," Rabobank cross-asset macro strategist Molly Schwartz said. Although core inflation has been trending lower, "they continually highlight that the risk to their inflation outlook is to the upside, and their inflation outlook is still materially above the 3% target for a few more quarters."
The Bank of Mexico called the rate cut a one-off move.

The bank said it "considers that maintaining the reference rate at the attained level for an extended period will support the convergence of inflation to its target and will be adequate to face the challenges posed by the external macroeconomic environment."
The disinflation process is continuing, the bank, adding that it still expects inflation to meet its 3% target in the fourth quarter of 2027.
Inflation accelerated to 3.62% in the first half of October from 3.42% in mid-September. Core inflation, which excludes fresh food and energy prices, was little changed at 3.78% in mid-October.

Economic activity also picked up after a small contraction at the start of the year, with gross domestic product expanding 1.4% seasonally adjusted in the second quarter from the first quarter, and 0.9% in the third quarter from the second.

Growth risks remain biased to the downside, and with continued slack conditions in the economy no demand-side inflation pressures are seen, while pass-through to prices from a weaker Mexican peso is expected to be limited, the Bank of Mexico said.

"The Bank of Mexico carried out the 'fine-tuning' and closed the door on an easing cycle in the same paragraph," Finamex chief economist Víctor Gómez Ayala said in a note.  "The bar for another cut is high and explicit: the board would have to abandon the guidance it gave today, and for that, core inflation would have to fall clearly below its forecast, not just meet it."
